messages.content: Write an internal post arguing for blameless postmortems at a company that does not do them yet. Around 250 words.

We Need to Start Running Blameless Postmortems

Four hours down last month, three teams scrambling, and once it was over nobody wrote up what happened. The ticket got closed and everyone moved on. That's the actual problem — not the outage itself.

When a postmortem can get you in trouble, people write around the truth. They leave out the detail that makes them look bad, they don't mention the near-miss they caught last week, and we end up missing exactly the information that would stop it from happening again.

Blameless doesn't mean nobody's accountable. It means the postmortem answers one question — what happened — and a separate process, run by managers, handles accountability. Nobody should have to wonder if an honest timeline becomes a line in their review.

The process itself isn't complicated. Build the timeline. Instead of "who broke this," ask "what made this decision look reasonable at the time." Assume everyone was acting on the information and systems in front of them, then go find where those failed. Write it up, share it internally, don't sand off the rough parts.

Google runs this way. So does Etsy, so does Netflix. Not because it's a nicer way to treat people — because it's the only method that actually catches the systemic stuff before it repeats. Ours is going to keep repeating until we change how we review it.

I'd like to pilot this on the next incident: a template, and a facilitator who wasn't on call for it. If it goes well, it becomes how we do this.

Got fifteen minutes at eng sync next week to talk it through?

output:
We Should Run Postmortems Without Blame

Last month we had four hours of downtime, three teams scrambling, and afterward: nothing. The ticket closed. Nobody wrote down what actually happened, so nobody else can learn from it.

That's the real problem. Not the outage — the silence after it.

When a postmortem might get you in trouble, you don't write the truth. You leave out the part where you weren't sure what the change would do. You skip the near-miss from last week because it never became an incident, so why bring it up. And the details we skip are exactly the ones that would stop this from happening again.

Blameless doesn't mean no accountability. It means the postmortem has one job — figure out what happened — and accountability is a separate conversation, between a manager and the people involved, not something that shows up as a paragraph in a shared doc. Nobody should have to choose between an honest timeline and their next review.

The mechanics are simple. Build the timeline. Ask "what made this look like the right call at the time," not "who broke it." Assume the person made a reasonable decision given what they knew, then go find where the systems or the information let them down. Write it up. Share it. Leave the rough edges in.

Google does this. Etsy does this. Netflix does this. Not out of kindness — because it's the only method that surfaces the systemic issue before it repeats. Ours already did.

I'd like to pilot it on the next incident — a template, and a facilitator who wasn't on call. Fifteen minutes at eng sync next week to talk it through?
